newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico and Venezuela to boost energy links.
newsitem.headline: Mexico and Venezuela to boost energy links.

text.p: Latin America's two main oil producers, Venezuela and Mexico, announced plans on Friday to boost energy cooperation, narrowing ties between two respective OPEC and non-OPEC powerhouses.
In a joint statement issued on a visit to Mexico by Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera, both countries said they planned "to intensify trade exchanges and joint investments in energy materials."
But the cooperation, to be designed by the nations' respective energy ministers, did not represent an "oil alliance," Caldera told a news conference.
He said it amounted to a "closening of ties" between his country, which is a key member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), and Mexico, which is a large non-OPEC producer.
Venezuela is considered Latin America's top petroleum producer in 1996, surpassing Mexico's Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) with an expected crude production average of 3.3 million barrels per day (bpd).
Pemex's final 1996 output levels were due to be announced next week and have to date been about 2.85 million bpd.
Caldera leaves Mexico on Saturday, returning to Caracas after a brief stopover in Guatemala.
He and Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo agreed to "a more active business sector participation" in energy projects that have for decades been mostly state run, Caldera said.

But the two leaders avoided tampering with the so-called San Jose Accord, under which Venezuela and Mexico supply oil at preferential terms to Central America to help it as it recovers from a decade of war in the 1980s.
The treaty was most recently renewed last August.
